processing: Niupi is first of all a local seed-grown tea variety, and no one fixed way of processing is documented. Made as green tea, it would be heated to stop oxidation, then shaped and dried.
harvest_season: Spring picking starts 7 to 10 days ahead of the local population variety, and its shoots grow strongly.
appearance_dry: No standard description is recorded; expect chunky shoots, given the variety's large, stout buds.
appearance_liquor: Typically yellow-green and clear, as with other Sichuan greens.
appearance_wet: Large, thick leaves and stout buds, in keeping with the variety.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting notes are documented. Thick-leaved Sichuan greens usually give a fuller, more robust cup than fine bud teas, and that is a reasonable expectation here.

brewing.notes: General advice for a sturdy-leaf green: start around 85°C and raise it slightly if the cup seems thin.

vintage_note: How it is sold is not well recorded. As with Chinese greens in general, look for the current spring harvest; the early start of this variety means first tea can come ahead of neighbouring gardens.
description:
Gulin Niupi is a seed-grown tea variety from Jiaozi Gully in Gulin County, in the south of Luzhou. Niupi means cowhide, and the name refers to its big, thick leaves. It is grown mainly in Gulin and nearby areas.

The practical interest for growers is its early, vigorous spring growth: picking starts 7 to 10 days before the local population plants, with fat, stout buds. As it is a seed-propagated population, plants may vary more than a clonal cultivar would.

Little is written about the finished tea itself. Thick-leaved Sichuan greens tend toward more body, so try a moderate temperature first and adjust from there.

The name is registered as a certification trademark for a geographical indication. If you meet it for sale, ask who made the tea and when it was picked, because the name describes the plant and the place more than a fixed style.
history: Records describe the plant rather than a story: a local population variety originating in Jiaozi Gully, Gulin, and counted among Sichuan's distinctive regional tea varieties, along with Chongzhou Pipa tea and Yunlian Zaobaijian. Little is documented about when it was first cultivated or who brought it to notice.
